replying_to: Replying to Understanding Judge Calibration in Multi-Turn Debates
display_title: Official Review of Submission5928 by Reviewer o4fq

summary.value:
* This paper studies the ability of LLM judges to accurately evaluate debates/arguments.
* The authors find that LLM judges are not well calibrated in their evaluations of which arguments are correct, and e.g. rate different arguments similarly.
* The authors then propose a finetuning strategy to better calibrate LLM judges, finding that this helps for improving LLM judge confident

strengths.value:
* Improving LLM judges is an important area for being able to continue to train models to be effective and safe, even as their capabilities grow more and more (especially at the point when LLMs exceed human capabilities on some domains). So this paper is looking into an important area/problem
* The result that LLMs aren’t effective judges is interesting/important (though I think similar results have been shown before). I think the result that models aren’t effective judges even after finetuning would be big if true

weaknesses.value:
* While the problem is important, I don’t think it’s that important for the reasons outlined in the paper (i.e., just as an evaluation task), and some of the more compelling motivations (for providing a scalable supervision signal for LLMs as they grow more and more capable) for having LLM judges are omitted from the intro.
* I found the paper very hard to follow, and e.g. didn’t follow the explanation for why a more sophisticated approach involving Gumbel distributions was needed over SFT. It really feels like simple SFT should be able to improve judge confidence, and rare that other approaches beat SFT when labels are available (especially by a large margin), so I think the bar for motivation and evidence for using anything other than SFT is high.
* It would be pretty helpful/illustrative to show some qualitative samples of what the arguments/debates look like (ideally in each domain), so the reader has a sense of what the debates look like. Otherwise, it’s a bit hard to picture or know what’s going on. It looks like there are a few at the very end of the appendix, but I think these are important enough to include in the main paper

questions.value: Can you explain in simple terms why you think SFT is not sufficient for getting good judges, and how the GFT procedure in these paper addresses that?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission5928 by Reviewer o4fq

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for providing feedback on the paper which is of utmost value to our work. Below we address your concerns in detail.


> While the problem is important, I don’t think it’s that important for the reasons outlined in the paper (i.e., just as an evaluation task), and some of the more compelling motivations (for providing a scalable supervision signal for LLMs as they grow more and more capable) for having LLM judges are omitted from the intro.

The central premise of the paper is to understand judge calibration in multi-turn debates. Towards this goal, we motivate the work by highlighting the pitfalls of LM judges (similar to humans) when rating debate arguments. We agree that our focus lies on an evaluation-based setting. Note that this is by design and even more important when compared to inducing additional pretraining signals. As our models become larger and more capable, the luxury of pretraining vanishes. In fact, recent works acknowledge that majority of scalable oversight is achieved during the post-training evaluation phase [1, 2, 3]. We build on this intuition and address the challenge of judge calibration during the post-training evaluation phase.

Regarding the utility of supervision signals, we agree that there is a need for new methods to selectively induce knowledge and reshape its information frontier. However, this remains a much broader industry-scale problem. A generalist supervised learner must be able to capture and compress per-token knowledge at scale, following the information bottleneck principle [4]. Thus, as the size of our datasets and models grows logarithmically, it becomes increasingly nontrivial to arrive at a general-purpose distillation strategy for both pretraining and post-training. With these aspects in mind, we focus on the post-training evaluation setting of multi-turn debates hoping that it would help in advancing our understanding for domain-specific tasks.

> I found the paper very hard to follow, and e.g. didn’t follow the explanation for why a more sophisticated approach involving Gumbel distributions was needed over SFT. It really feels like simple SFT should be able to improve judge confidence, and rare that other approaches beat SFT when labels are available (especially by a large margin), so I think the bar for motivation and evidence for using anything other than SFT is high.

Since GFT builds a distributional perspective on the paradigm of SFT, at the core of our approach we conduct supervised finetuning for a fixed number of iterations. Note that the paper does not propose an alternative to SFT neither we intend to replace SFT for most language modelling tasks. Our setting and study addresses miscalibration. Towards this end, we equip SFT with a mixture of gumbels distribution constructed using score and confidence ratings as features for sampling. Simply put, GFT still conducts SFT albeit from a different exponential distribution. Thus, we make no changes to the learning paradigm itself, but we only change the space from which the finetuning signal arises.

It is nontrivial to calibrate for confidence using SFT on the original dataset. This is because of two reasons. (1) SFT, as a finetuning signal, is agnostic to the uncertainty present in the dataset. Maximizing log-likelihood over a set of tokens may not necessarily calibrate for the confidence associated to selecting those tokens. (2) Empirically, SFT is notorious in overfitting towards similar tokens. Keeping these two aspects in mind, we recall our empirical insights about SFT observed in the paper. (line 296) "Llama finetuned with SFT, on the other hand, does not follow the trend. SFT minimizes the score-confidence gaps to values lower than 1 for 97% of arguments. Intuitively, SFT forces judge models to raise score ratings such that judges yield score ≈ confidence. This behavior is validated by observing the high ECE of SFT indicating lower reliability in calibration." As we observe, conducting SFT on the base distribution naively forces judge models to raise the score and match confidence. However, _raising the score rating is not the same as minimizing overconfidence_. We thus require a quantity that captures uncertainty in both score and confidence. Gumbel distributions explicitly model the uncertainty and using the left tail of these distributions allows us to sample debate arguments that are well-calibrated for score and confidence. This is the reason why GFT leads to a balance between the score and confidence, by explicitly minimizing overconfidence.

display_title: Official Review of Submission5928 by Reviewer SZca

summary.value: The paper proposes to study the calibration of judge’s final judgments in an LLM debate setup. LLM debates have been shown to be useful for producing more truthful final judgments of human and LLM judges (judges are shown transcripts of debates between LLMs). To the best of my understanding, experiments elicit a numerical confidence score (as textual output) from the judge alongside its numerical rating for the proposition under debate (as textual output). The paper poses that there is an issue when the rating does not match the confidence score. This is called the score-confidence gap. A second metric, the Expected Calibration Error, is defined based on a distance between the judge confidence ratings and the output of some accuracy quantity acc(.,.) — not sure I am following this part. A third metric, the Brier score, is computed between the judge confidence score and a human confidence score. After showing that there are issues with judge calibration according to these metrics, the paper proposes a finetuning method that works by oversampling certain regimes of the distribution of LLM debates. A model trained on such an oversampled distribution, rather than a more straightforward SFT approach, achieves better calibrated judge confidences under the reported metrics.

strengths.value: - Important: The paper addresses an interesting topic, the calibration of judges in LLM debate experiments. We should hope that debate not only improves judge accuracy, but also improves judge calibration.

weaknesses.value:
- Very important: I find the core measurements in the paper quite confusing. To the best my of understanding, the central premise is that the rating scores should match the confidence scores. I do not see why that should be the case. When I am reviewing a paper for ICLR, I give a rating score and a confidence score — why should these scores match? Let’s zoom out a bit: judges could give a full probability distribution over the range of scores, 1-10. Then there are many ways one might think of confidence. You could compute confidence as entropy, and get a rating as the expected value of this distribution. What is the elicited confidence score supposed to represent? The probability of the rating, p(rating), of that full distribution? Or something else? The paper does not provide sufficient justification for this core premise.
- Very important: It is not optional to include information about the human ratings used in the study. Where did these people come from? What were they told to do? How many humans rated each debate? Did they have pre-existing opinions on the debate topics — did debates move their ratings up or down? These details are crucial to understanding the meaning of the data used in this paper. Moreover, I could not describe the human ratings as a “ground truth oracle” for subjective debate topics like those studied in the paper, even if all the above details were provided. As a result, I find it very difficult to interpret the ECE and Brier scores used.

questions.value:
Please do try to clarify the motivation behind the score-confidence gap and other calibration metrics used in the paper.

On the related work, for the "Uncertainty in Language Models" section, this is a nice tour of recent papers from Anthropic but it does not go into much depth on work on uncertainty. I'd recommend looking into https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.14983 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.05221

comment.value:
Thank you for your feedback. Below we address your concerns in detail.

> Very important: I find the core measurements in the paper quite confusing. To the best my of understanding, the central premise is that the rating scores should match the confidence scores. I do not see why that should be the case. When I am reviewing a paper for ICLR, I give a rating score and a confidence score — why should these scores match? Let’s zoom out a bit: judges could give a full probability distribution over the range of scores, 1-10. Then there are many ways one might think of confidence. You could compute confidence as entropy, and get a rating as the expected value of this distribution. What is the elicited confidence score supposed to represent? The probability of the rating, p(rating), of that full distribution? Or something else? The paper does not provide sufficient justification for this core premise.

Respected reviewer, we are a bit confused with your concern. Given that you highlighted the problem setting and topic of calibration as a _strength_ of our work ["Important: The paper addresses an interesting topic, the calibration of judges in LLM debate experiments.", "We should hope that debate not only improves judge accuracy, but also improves judge calibration."], we are unable to understand your confusion. Please clarify your concern while we make a comprehensive attempt below to clarify it.

Typical evaluation settings for LMs involve both a score and confidence rating. From a probabilistic perspective, The score quantifies the accuracy that logits are correct. Similarly, the confidence quantifies our beliefs in that accuracy. This way confidence can represent various formulations such as entropy, likelihood or correlation. In our setting this corresponds to p(rating). Following your example of the ICLR reviewing process. Each reviewer can have a different notion of confidence, i.e- the reviewer can interpret it as accuracy of score rating, assessment of your own capabilities, etc. Similarly, we query judge LMs to output a score and confidence corresponding to their evaluation. This is explained in line 190 and Section 1. We do not explicitly specify LMs to provide their definition of confidence. Rather, we interpret confidence as the probability of a given rating following prior works in calibration literature [1, 2]. Additional details on the structure and dataset prompts can be found in Appendix C along with qualitative examples in Appendix D.

Similarly, following prior works in calibration [1], we expect confidence to be proportional to the score rating. That is the definition of a calibrated model. In the case of ICLR reviews, an evaluation with high score and high confidence rating is more reliable when compared to an evaluation with high score and low confidence. Similarly, an evaluation with low score and low confidence rating is more reliable when compared to an evaluation with low score and high confidence. That is, under-confident and over-confident evaluations loose reliability in the evaluation process. This forms the core aspect of calibration in language modelling which has been followed by recent works in evaluation literature [2].

Thank you for raising the concern. We have added details about human raters in Appendix C. We recruited a total of 10 human raters as debate judges. Human raters are aged between 20 to 40 years old and familiar with common world events. Each rater rated all 20 debates per model, i.e- $20 \times 4 = 80$ total debates. Since each debate consists of 10 rounds per side, i.e- 20 arguments in total, each human rater provided $80 \times 20 = 1600$ ratings for score and confidence each. Thus, the dataset consists of $1600 \times 10 = 16000$ human ratings. Note that human raters do not possess strong opinions about debate topics prior to evaluation. However, human raters are well-versed in world events and thus, similar to LM judges, are aware of worldly facts and possess their own preferences. In the interest of anonymity, we will only be able to disclose the origin of human raters in the camera-ready version. Regarding the instructions provided to each human rater, these remain the same as other LM judges as we mentioned previously in Appendix C. Finally, debates did not move their ratings up or down. The human raters were required to rate these debates independently and to the best of their abilities.

Regarding the ground-truth aspect of human ratings, each human rater is well-versed in day-to-day worldly events and thus possesses decisive abilities akin to LM judges. Furthermore, human judges are apriori well-calibrated as they balance confidence ratings corresponding to their ability to provide a faithful rating. Furthermore, in line with prior works that utilize humans as oracles for subjective tasks (ChatGPT for human preferences) and preferential learning (Llama distillation) [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], we fix human judges as our ground-truth. This is empirically validated upon observing ideal calibration and lowest overconfidence among human judges (Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4).

Please let us know if the response above addressed your concerns.

summary.value: The authors discuss the calibration of language model (LM) judges in multi-turn debates, highlighting issues of overconfidence in their ratings and propose a Gumbel Fine-Tuning (GFT) strategy to improve the calibration of LM judges by focusing on lower confidences and scores.

strengths.value:
The paper follows a clear strucutre and is well written. 
The authors systematically show that model confidence increases over debate rounds while scores decrease, across multiple frontier and smaller models. The proposed Gumbel Finetuning (GFT) is an original approach that leverages the tail of the data distribution to fine-tune calibration.

weaknesses.value:
The paper only examines a limited number of models and debates for 10 rounds on five different topics. Only a Llama 3.2 3B model was fine-tuned in the experiments, so it remains unclear if GFT scales to larger judges. Additionally, it is unclear whether the gap between confidence and scores negatively affects the performance of LM judges or if they perform better after GFT fine-tuning. The scope of the paper is narrow because the authors only examine calibration in multi-turn self-debates.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for providing feedback on the paper which is of utmost value to our work. Below we address your concerns in detail.

> The paper only examines a limited number of models and debates for 10 rounds on five different topics. Only a Llama 3.2 3B model was fine-tuned in the experiments, so it remains unclear if GFT scales to larger judges.

Our problem setting consists of maximum 10 rounds as these are already beyond the natural standard of an international human debate competition. The World Universities Debating Championship (WUDC), which is the gold standard of international debates, holds only 9 rounds over 3 days. Our experiments investigated finetuning models with longer debate rounds (15 and 20 rounds). However, models were found to hallucinate factual arguments, make incorrect statements and deviate frequently from their original stance (i.e- for or against the motion). Thus, we empirically found 10 rounds suitable for both frontier as well as open-source models.

Note that our setting does not simply train on five different topics, these are five different _categories_ (line 161). In total, our finetuning dataset has 20 long-form debates per model, i.e- 20 topics. We would like to highlight that while we utilize 20 debates, these debates are long-form turn-by-turn debates obtained from each _model_. To put this in perspective, we have a total of $20 \text{(debates)} \times 10 \text{(rounds)} \times 2 \text{(sides per round)} \times 4 \text{(models)} \times 500 \text{(tokens per argument)} = 800K$ tokens which is of the scale of data required to finetune both open-sourced and closed frontier LMs such as Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-7B (on Spider dataset), GPT-4o-mini, GPT-oss 20B and GPT-3.5. Since our experiments finetune 3B parameter models (Llama 3.2 3B), we are already in the regime of a larger finetuning dataset for the given 3B model size (as per finetuning scaling laws).

Finally, while our main focus of evaluation is the Llama 3.2 3B model, we highlight that the 3B parameter regime (and this model) is sufficient for domain-specific exploration. Since we are focussing on the domain of debates, we are interested in subject matter comprehension and response to structured critique. Models of the order of 1B parameters and beyond possess these capabilities. We thus choose the 3B variant due to a lack of other general-purpose and versatile models beyond the 1B regime. Additionally, note that we finetune multiple Llama 3.2 3B models corresponding to different hyperparameter settings, data splits and ablation studies. Specifically, we finetune atleast $8 \text{(ablations)} \times 5 + 8 \text{(hyperparameters)} \times 5 + 2 \text{(data splits)} \times 5 = 210$ 3B model runs. Thus, we argue that the scale of our experiments, albeit centered on a particular model behavior, is comprehensive in its evaluation.

Please also refer to our response to reviewer NgiY.

> Additionally, it is unclear whether the gap between confidence and scores negatively affects the performance of LM judges or if they perform better after GFT fine-tuning.

Since GFT builds a distributional perspective on the paradigm of SFT, at the core of our approach we conduct finetuning for a fixed number of iterations. Early stopping and a slower learning rate are utilized which prevent the model from overfitting towards our debate data distribution. It is because of this problem setting, we do not observe any drop in performance of the base model from its original behavior. GFT leads to a more nuanced balance between the score and confidence. Models lower score ratings in cases where other judges were overconfident of their score. However, this balance in score-confidence ratings does not trade off with the language modeling capability of finetuned judges. That is, models continue to maintain a baseline level of text summarization and question-answering ability.

> The scope of the paper is narrow because the authors only examine calibration in multi-turn self-debates.

We focus on the problem of calibration in multi-turn debates as it is given less attention from a linguistic perspective. In fact, we do acknowledge in Section 6 (Limitations) that the setting is restricted to multi-turn debates. We believe that the setting is representative of long-form dialog tasks. Studying calibration in such a setting allows us to frely study other less explored degrees of freedom such as choice and structure of debater arguments, preference towards a particular topic and deviation from human raters. Furthermore, emerging literature has shown that calibration continues to be a persisting issue even in frontier models [1]. LM judges remain uncertain of their ratings or conceal their overall confidence. This becomes increasingly worrysome for models that are used as day-to-day conversational and dialog agents for personal use. We thus believe focussing the scope towards calibration and investigating it from a linguistic perspective in debates uncovers many facets that were not observed before. 


> Is the small 5.56% ECE improvement statistically significant across multiple seeds or runs?

Thank you for raising the concern. In order to strengthen evaluation metrics, we have added error bars in Table 1 for al columns. Error bars are reported over 5 random runs wherein each run was independently executed and reported. All evaluation is reported on a heldout set of 5 debates which do not possess any overlap in topic or argument types as the training dataset. We present the mean and standard deviation as entries in Table 1. We observe that the 5.56% improvement is consistent and significant across 5 random runs.

> Small comments:

Thank you for the suggestions, we have fixed these in the revised manuscript.

Kindly let us know if the response above addressed your concerns. We would be happy to clarify any further concerns that remain.

display_title: Official Review of Submission5928 by Reviewer Ng1Y

summary.value: This paper studies judge calibration in multi-turn LLM debates, specifically, the mismatch between model-assigned scores and their self-reported confidence. The authors show that LMs acting as judges tend to become over-confident. They propose Gumbel Finetuning (GFT), intended to improve calibration by focusing on low-confidence/low-scores.

strengths.value:
-  **[Problem importance]** The paper addresses an important issue in LLM evaluation, namely judge calibration.
- **[Wide model coverage]** While the overall experimental scope is quite limited (20 total debates) the authors make use of a wide range of model families.
- **[Clarity/presentation]** The paper is well-structured and clearly outlines the methodology, motivation, and approach.
- **[Somewhat novel observations]** Although issues with calibration and confidence have been widely studied in the single agent and single-turn (ensamble) settings, the observation of overconfidence drift in multi-turn debates is new.

weaknesses.value:
- **[Minimal methodological novelty]:** The proposed GFT is a simple rejection-sampling heuristic applied to SFT; it doesn’t constitute a new calibration framework. While the motivation for the rejection clear, I would have liked to see a deeper connection established between the confidence distributions present in the training data and the subsequent distributions produced by the model.
- **[Limited experimental scope]:** Only 20 debates are used throughout the paper. It is extremely difficult to appreciate the generality of these the observed trends with such a small sample size. 
- **[Shallow analysis]:** Beyond the issue of small experiental scope, the paper also does not dig into *why* overconfidence arises, or how this overconfidence differs from existing analysis in the case of single agents or single turn aggregation. Are we simply making the same observations as prior work (e.g., Zheng et al. 2023; Guo et al. 2017; Zhu et al. 2025), and the multi-turn aspect is just an red herring? I would have liked to see this better contextualized. Similarly its not clear how GFT actually addresses this issue, beyond some high level intuition regarding rare events. 
- **Evaluation metrics are weak:** ECE and Brier scores are reported without confidence or significance tests, making the improvements difficult to interpret (I assume this is the result of the small sample size).

We thank the reviewer for providing feedback on the paper which is of utmost value to our work. Below we address your concerns in detail.

> [Minimal methodological novelty]: The proposed GFT is a simple rejection-sampling heuristic applied to SFT; it doesn’t constitute a new calibration framework. While the motivation for the rejection clear, I would have liked to see a deeper connection established between the confidence distributions present in the training data and the subsequent distributions produced by the model.

We would like to highlight that GFT consists of two main aspects. (1) Firstly, the feature construction phase populates score and confidence ratings as parametric features for the gumbel distribution. Note that unlike computationally expensive embedding schemes, we rely on raw and rich informative features obtained directly from text. (2) Secondly, the sampling phase employs a novel mixture of gumbels formulation. Sampling is carried out from the left tail of this mixture distribution. While we combine these aspects with SFT, we would like to highlight that the core contribution of our work is not alter/surpass SFT. We aim to _understand_ judge calibration and to that end, the study combines our feature pooling and sampling framework with SFT. To the best of our knowledge, feature pooling (from raw confidence ratings) and mixture of gumbels sampling are novel formulations within the context LMs as judges.

Regarding the connection between confidence distributions of training dataset and the model, we would like to remind the reviewer that these comparisons are already available as part of Figures 3 and 4. Since the dataset consists of primarily human ratings, we can exactly compare human confidence ratings with GFT confidence values. In Figure 3, we observe that finetuning using mixture of gumbels combined with feature pooling leads to a reduction in overconfidence and balanced ratings for both score and confidence when compared to SFT. In Figure 4, we observe that while the confidence distribution of human judges tends to the under-confident region, frontier and frozen LM judges tend to be overconfident. GFT finetuned Llama 3.2 judges rejection sample from their left tail and better calibrate confidence with their score distributions. _Intuitivley, sampling from the mixture of gumbels estimator is akin to conducting rao-blackwellization (minimizing variance) over debate arguments by utilizing pooled features as additional conditional information._

> [Limited experimental scope]: Only 20 debates are used throughout the paper. It is extremely difficult to appreciate the generality of these the observed trends with such a small sample size.

We clarify that we simulate _20 debates per model_, i.e- in total we have $20 \times 4 = 80$ long-form debates. We would like to highlight that while we utilize 20 debates, these debates are long-form turn-by-turn debates obtained from each _model_. To put this in perspective, we have a total of $20 \text{(debates)} \times 10 \text{(rounds)} \times 2 \text{(sides per round)} \times 4 \text{(models)} \times 500 \text{(tokens per argument)} = 800K$ tokens which is of the scale of data required to finetune both open-sourced and closed frontier LMs such as Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-7B (on Spider dataset), GPT-4o-mini, GPT-oss 20B and GPT-3.5. Since our experiments finetune 3B parameter models (Llama 3.2 3B), we are already in the regime of a larger finetuning dataset for the given 3B model size (as per finetuning scaling laws). Regarding the generality of trends, we note that our data distribution consists of multiple modes in topics, argument types, opinions, narrative styles and ratings. Specifically, the distribution consists of over 1600 phrased arguments corresponding to 4 frontier models. This diversity plays a key role in tuning general-purpose debate judges.

I would have liked to see this better contextualized. Similarly its not clear how GFT actually addresses this issue, beyond some high level intuition regarding rare events.

We refer the reviewer to the last paragraph of page 4. The discussion provided explicitly dissects potential causes of model overconfidence in LM judges. We begin by empirically studying the variation of judge ratings as debates progress over rounds (Figure 1 and Section 4). We then move deeper to assess this variation for different debates and argument types (Figure 2 and Section 4). Combined these empirical results and the intuition from Figure 3, we discuss and expand on the main cuases of overconfidence being a preference for critical and structured arguments (subject matter comprehension). Intuitively, different models have different preferences over how the debate argument is structured and critiqued. Note that this is different from past results which attribute LMs demonstrating preferences towards text formatting (punctuation, abbreviations and sentence conciseness) and narrative style.

Section 5 characterizes the operation of GFT and its key role in addressing overconfidence. A straightforward way to address overconfidence in LM judges would be to construct the distribution of well-calibrated arguments (tail samples). This can be achieved by fitting a Gaussian distribution and iteratively sampling from its left tail. However, this strategy requires a large number of arguments to expressively represent the left tail of the data distribution. Simply put, this is analogous to obtaining access to a part of the pretraining dataset frontier models were trained on. Thus, completing the left tail becomes infeasible in real-world deployed systems due to the scale and high-dimensional nature of distributions models were trained on. GFT, on the other hand, leverages the statistical structure of judge ratings to approximate the left tail of dataset. We model the dataset as a collection of extreme values of score and confidence ratings. This is carried out by utilizing the multivariate Gumbel distribution to serve as a proxy for dataset samples. The Gumbel distribution, being the distribution of extremes, allows us to expressively model the tail of the dataset. It is precisely due to the structure of left-tail of the Gumbel distribution, we are able to squash down the calibration gap in the rating space. Additionally, the distribution presents a flexible and tractable form for sampling during the inference step. This further allows us to formulate the mixture of gumbels distribution which does not lead to any exploding values or mode collapse during the sampling process.

> Evaluation metrics are weak: ECE and Brier scores are reported without confidence or significance tests, making the improvements difficult to interpret (I assume this is the result of the small sample size).

Thank you for raising the concern. In order to strengthen evaluation metrics, we have added error bars in Table 1 for all columns. Error bars are reported over 5 random runs wherein each run was independently executed and reported. All evaluation is reported on a heldout set of 5 debates which do not possess any overlap in topic or argument types as the training dataset. We present the mean and standard deviation as entries in Table 1. Table 1 demonstrates that both ECE and Brier scores present consistent trends. Values for frozen models persist towards larger calibration error whereas SFT finetuned models stagnate towards a fixed value. GFT, provides improvements in calibration error and is empirically found to be more consistent than its counterparts.

Kindly let us know if the response above addressed your concerns. We would be happy to clarify any further concerns that remain.

summary.value:
This paper investigates calibration of LLM judges in multi-turn debate settings, identifying a divergence between assigned scores and self-reported confidence. The authors introduce GFT as a method intended to mitigate this score–confidence gap. Reviewers generally agree that the topic is timely and potentially important. However, there is consistent concern across reviews regarding: the conceptual framing of calibration; the motivation and interpretation of the proposed metrics; the limited experimental scope and generality; and whether GFT provides substantive advantages over standard SFT.

While the rebuttal addresses several issues related to presentation and clarity, the central conceptual disagreements, particularly concerning the meaning of confidence and its relationship to scores, remain unresolved. Given the competitiveness of the venue, these unresolved issues substantially weaken the case for acceptance.

reviewer_concerns.value:
**Concerns Addressed:**
* The authors added error bars, clarified dataset scale in terms of tokens and arguments, and included qualitative examples. These changes improve transparency and presentation.
* Additional information regarding the number and demographics of human raters was provided, partially addressing concerns about annotation transparency.
* The rebuttal clarifies that GFT is intended as a sampling-based augmentation of SFT rather than a replacement. This helps clarify intent, though it does not fully resolve concerns about novelty.

**Concerns Still Outstanding:**
* Multiple reviewers remain unconvinced that confidence should be proportional to rating or that mismatches necessarily imply miscalibration. 
* The meaning of ECE and Brier scores in subjective debate settings remains unclear. In particular, treating human ratings as a meaningful ground truth for calibration in such contexts remains contentious.
* GFT is still perceived as a lightweight sampling heuristic layered on top of SFT, with insufficient theoretical or empirical justification for why it is necessary or clearly superior to standard SFT.
* Experiments are confined to multi turn self debates and largely to a single 3B model, making claims about broader applicability and scalable oversight appear overstated.
* It remains unclear whether improvements in calibration metrics lead to meaningful gains in judging behavior or downstream performance.

**Overall:**
While the topic is timely and the empirical observations are potentially interesting, the paper does not meet the bar for acceptance at a highly selective venue. The conceptual foundations of the proposed calibration definition and metrics remain disputed, and the empirical evidence is insufficient to justify the claimed significance or generality of the proposed method.
